questions.question: How do Rails models and migrations work together?
questions.title: Rails Models and Migrations
questions.direct_answer: A model (app/models/user.rb, class User < ApplicationRecord) is the Ruby class that maps to a database table and gives you the query methods and validations. A migration is the Ruby file that creates or changes that table (the schema). They work together: the migration creates the users table and its columns; the model is the Ruby code you interact with that reads and writes those rows. The model is the behavior; the migration is the structure. You generate both with rails g model User name:string, which creates the migration AND an empty model file.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you distinguish the model (behavior, Ruby class) from the migration (structure, schema change) and know rails g model creates both.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the model 'is' the table, or editing the model file to change columns (you change the schema via a migration).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: The model is the Ruby class (behavior); the migration is the schema change (structure). rails g model creates both; you change columns via new migrations, not the model.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define Rails Models and Migrations simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: The model (app/models/user.rb) is the Ruby class — behavior: validations, associations, methods.
The migration (db/migrate) is the schema change — structure: create_table, add_column, add_index.
rails g model User name:string creates BOTH a migration and an empty model file.
Change columns via a new migration, not by editing the model file.
The model reads/writes the table the migration created.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A Rails model — app/models/user.rb, class User inherits ApplicationRecord — is the Ruby class that maps to a database table and gives you the query methods, validations, and associations. A migration is the Ruby file that creates or changes that table, the schema. They work together: the migration creates the users table and its columns; the model is the Ruby code you interact with that reads and writes those rows. The model is the behavior; the migration is the structure. You generate both at once with rails g model User name string, which creates the migration file and an empty model file you then fill with validations and associations. A common mistake is thinking the model is the table, when the model is the Ruby class and the table is the schema, or editing the model file to add a column, when you should change the schema via a new migration.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A model (app/models/user.rb, class User < ApplicationRecord) is the Ruby class that maps to a database table and gives you the query methods and validations.

A migration is the Ruby file that creates or changes that table (the schema).

They work together: the migration creates the users table and its columns; the model is the Ruby code you interact with that reads and writes those rows. The model is the behavior; the migration is the structure. You generate both with rails g model User name:string, which creates the migration AND an empty model file.

Thinking the model 'is' the table, or editing the model file to change columns (you change the schema via a migration).

sections.title: Model and Migration Together
sections.content:
The migration builds the table; the model is the class you use to read/write it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G[rails g model User] --> M[migration: create users table]
  G --> C[model: class User < ApplicationRecord]
  C -->|reads/writes| T[users table built by M]
```

sections.title: Generating and using a model + migration
sections.content:
```ruby
# Generate BOTH a model and its migration:
#   rails g model User name:string email:string
# Creates:
#   db/migrate/<ts>_create_users.rb  (the migration - structure)
#   app/models/user.rb              (the model - behavior)

class CreateUsers < ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]
  def change
    create_table :users do |t|     # STRUCTURE: the table and columns
      t.string :name
      t.string :email
      t.timestamps
    end
  end
end

class User < ApplicationRecord     # BEHAVIOR: validations, associations
  validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true
  has_many :posts
end
```
